newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African banks prepare for foreign accounts.
newsitem.headline: S.African banks prepare for foreign accounts.

text.p: South African banks are preparing to take advantage of relaxed foreign exchange controls and introduce foreign-denominated domestic accounts in July, but without any indication of the likely demand.

First National Bank, Standard, Nedcor and ABSA all said they had systems in place to register foreign-denominated accounts as soon as the central Reserve Bank sets the conditions and gives the go-ahead.
Bankers expect the Reserve Bank to set a ceiling of around 160,000 rand - twice the increased annual travel allowance of 80,000 rand - for individual foreign currency holdings.
But they complain that the Reserve Bank has declined so far to spell out limits or to say whether individuals may hold both domestic and offshore accounts or only one or the other.

"We would have hoped to have had the information earlier, but we're hoping now to get it from the Reserve Bank before the end of this week," said Standard Corporate and Merchant Bank international division director Owen Tidbury.
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel announced in his March 12 budget speech that South African residents would, for the first time, be allowed to hold foreign currencies from July 1.
He said the conditions would be spelled out after meetings with senior bankers, who were briefed initially on March 13.
The concession was part of a major relaxation of remaining controls on residents.
At least four major banks have started to advertise or prepare advertisements for foreign currency acccounts and at least one has started to mail out application forms.
"Obviously we can do nothing until the 1st of July, but we would have the information to open your account," said Tidbury.
First National Bank head of finance and administration John Muggeridge said he had prepared programmes to manage foreign currency call accounts and term accounts of up to 12 months.
"As soon as we get the go-ahead from the Reserve Bank, we can start opening accounts," he said.
All the banks said they were looking at floating interest call accounts and a range of fixed-interest term accounts for periods of up to 12 months.
"We have not taken a decision yet on how many currencies we will offer - maybe four or five," said ABSA head of international operations Wolf Kammerer.
A Nedcor spokesman said the bank planned to offer call accounts denominated in at least 20 currencies.
All the banks said they would impose minimum balance and transaction restrictions to protect themselves against the high cost of foreign exchange transactions.
The most commonly mentioned minumum level was 5,000 rand with Standard's Tidbury saying a 1,000 pound or 2,500 dollar minimum might be considered.
Tidbury said that on the basis of rates offered by Standard's overseas division, overnight rates could be around 2.6 percent rising to 4.125 percent on a 12-month deposit.
Bankers said it was impossible to predict how much foreign currency South Africans might hold in domestic accounts.
Muggeridge said: "There is a pent-up interest in this sort of investment that we have still to measure."
Tidbury added: "There is absolutely no factual information on which to base an assessment of the likely demand."
Kammerer said travellers assuming a steady depreciation of the rand might hedge their savings, but predicted that demand would fall after an initial surge of interest in July.
Most bankers said they would convert the rand deposits as soon as they were made and invest in the source economy.
"The rand-to-dollar risk factor would be carried by the depositor. Frankly I think that is where the main incentive from a South African perspective would be - as a rand hedge," said Tidbury.
But Kammerer said significant deposits could be useful to banks seeking to avoid the premium on foreign borrowings.
"If the pool is big and you have a certain hard core which can be used for short-term financing then there is a little benefit in that for the bank," he said.
